title.en: Sexual reproduction in plants and humans
From flower to fruit, from cell to baby

text.en: A flower, a fruit and a baby all come from fertilisation, the joining of two cells. Sexual reproduction mixes DNA from two parents.

Sexual reproduction involves two parents and gametes, which fuse to form a zygote. DNA mixing produces variation.
A flower has sepals, petals, stamens (male: anther and filament) and pistil (female: stigma, style and ovary).
Pollination moves pollen from anther to stigma by wind, water or insects. Self-pollination is within one flower; cross-pollination is between flowers.
Fertilisation: a pollen tube carries male gametes to the ovule. The zygote becomes an embryo, the ovule becomes a seed and the ovary becomes a fruit.
Human male: testes make sperm and testosterone, the vas deferens carries sperm, and glands add fluid to make semen.
Human female: ovaries release an egg, the fallopian tube is the site of fertilisation, and the uterus holds the embryo; the placenta gives nourishment.
If the egg is not fertilised, the uterine lining breaks down in menstruation every month.
Reproductive health: contraceptive methods prevent pregnancy; barrier methods like condoms also reduce sexually transmitted infections. Sex ratio matters, and sex-selective abortion is illegal.

problem.en: Describe the changes in a flower after fertilisation.

text.en: The zygote develops into an embryo inside the ovule.
The ovary becomes the fruit, and petals and sepals wither.

prompt.en: How does sexual reproduction occur in flowers and humans?

points.en: Pollination moves pollen to the stigma; fertilisation joins the gametes.
Ovule becomes seed, ovary becomes fruit.
In humans, fertilisation occurs in the fallopian tube; the embryo implants in the uterus.
